name: Latchel

gate1.read: If you're a Latchel customer, you can create your API key yourself today, right from the Latchel console. Nothing in Latchel's published materials says the API, webhooks, sandbox, or MCP connector cost extra or need a certain plan.

gate2.read: Through the API you can push work orders into Latchel from your own system, keep properties, residents, owners, and vendors in sync, attach photos, cancel early-stage jobs, and approve or deny budgets. Webhooks tell you when jobs, residents, properties, invoices, or files change. The published documentation shows no API way to mark a job complete, schedule it, change the vendor after creation, or read and post work-order notes. Coverage is 71.59%, write coverage is 50%, and completing a work order (a critical item) scores 0, so gate 2 holds the letter at B.

mcp.note: Latchel runs an official, Latchel-hosted MCP server that reads and acts on work orders, tasks, properties, and residents, and you connect it by signing in with your own Latchel account (OAuth), so the one-step bump applied: 84 (B) to 87 (B+).

reads.c2: This is a normal, well-structured REST API with clear rate limits and a documented "only what changed" sync, which suits a nightly sync into a spreadsheet, database, or Zapier flow. Be careful with retries and paging: the published documentation shows no protection against creating the same work order twice and no overwrite protection, and following the API's own "next page" link can skip records unless you add the page size back yourself. There is no public status page and no request ID to quote in support tickets.
reads.c3: There is one full-access key per company, so you can't give an app or AI agent a limited, read-only, or second key through the Partner API, and replacing the key breaks every integration using it. You can rotate the key yourself, and you can connect Claude or ChatGPT through Latchel's own sign-in instead of sharing the key. A sandbox exists (the live tests for this report ran there, not on production), but the documentation doesn't say how to get its key.
reads.c4: An AI coding tool can load Latchel's OpenAPI file and build against the whole API, and Latchel's own connector lets Claude or ChatGPT read and act on work orders. The AI-friendly help files leave out the endpoint reference itself. API changes are announced inside general product release notes, not a dedicated API changelog.

checklist.note: List, create, read, update, and cancel work orders. Listing and reading worked in live tests.
You can read a job's state and its history and get webhooks on changes. Only cancel, approve, and deny can be written.
A vendor can be set only when the job is created, not on an existing job. Per-property and per-portfolio vendor priority rules are writable.
Create, read, update, and delete vendor companies, plus vendor users and service zip codes.
The scheduled window and resident availability are readable, but the published documentation shows no way to set or change a schedule through the API.
List, read, add to a property, update, and set move dates.
List, create, read, update, and merge properties, plus portfolios.

checklist.item: Photos or attachments on a work order
checklist.note: List, upload, read, and reclassify files on a job, including before and after photos.

checklist.item: Messages or comments on a work order
checklist.note: Intake transcripts are readable, but the published documentation shows no way to read or post work-order notes or messages.
Your PMS job, property, unit, and user ids can be written onto Latchel records.
Permission to enter and access instructions are writable on jobs, with default access instructions on properties and portfolios.
Estimate fields are read-only and filled in only while a job waits on approval. Adding an estimate is documented only for the MCP connector.
List and read invoices, plus an invoice webhook. Vendors submit invoices, so reading them is what this item needs.
Owner records and budget approve or deny exist, but the published documentation shows no owner-approval record in the API.
Create a work order with POST /jobs.
A vendor can be assigned only when the work order is created.
The published documentation shows no API way to mark a work order complete. Confirming completion is documented only for the MCP connector.
Cancel with POST /jobs/{id}/cancel, allowed only before dispatch or while a job awaits approval.
The published documentation shows no API way to change the vendor on an existing job. Latchel documents it as a dashboard action.

checklist.item: Approve or reject an estimate or invoice
checklist.note: Approve a job's budget (with a note and a maximum cost) or deny it.

checks.title: Object coverage
checks.why: Objects earn 22 of 28 weighted points. Work orders, vendors, residents, properties, photos, PMS links, entry instructions, and invoices are fully covered; status changes, assignment, scheduling, notes, estimates, and owner approval are partial.

checks.title: Write coverage
checks.why: Creating a work order works (1.0) and assigning works only at creation (0.5), but the published documentation shows no API way to complete one (0.0), for 4.5 of 9 weighted points.

checks.title: Lifecycle coverage
checks.why: Cancelling an early-stage job and approving or denying a budget both work, 5 of 7 weighted points. The published documentation shows no API way to reassign the vendor.

checks.title: Change notification
checks.why: Webhooks fire on create and update for jobs, residents, portfolios, invoices, properties, files, owners, and on-call alerts, covering 90.2% of the critical and important weight. Changed-since polling also works on jobs, properties, and residents.

checks.title: Modern API conventions
checks.why: Standard resource-based REST with JSON and GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, described in an OpenAPI 3.0 file. JSON responses were confirmed in live reads.

checks.title: Consistent typing
checks.why: Ids and flags are typed consistently on core records, and live reads matched. But money fields such as maximum cost and estimate are plain decimal numbers, some fields differ between the API and webhooks, and job timestamps have no time zone.

checks.title: Structured errors
checks.why: Errors use correct status codes and a JSON body with a readable message, confirmed live for a missing key, a bad key, a missing record, and bad inputs. No stable machine-readable error code is documented or returned.

checks.title: Duplicate prevention
checks.why: The published documentation shows no idempotency key or other duplicate protection on creates. Two sandbox jobs share the same reference id, so that id does not stop duplicates.

checks.title: Graceful handling under load
checks.why: A documented limit of 600 requests per key per 10 minutes, with a 429 reply, Retry-After, and a reset header. Rate-limit headers appeared on ordinary live reads; no 429 was triggered.

checks.title: Pagination for large collections
checks.why: Page-number paging up to 500 per page with a next-page link is documented. But following that link as returned drops the page size, which skipped records in a live test, and job lists have no stated order or total.

checks.title: Bulk or incremental export
checks.why: A documented "Delta Sync" returns only what changed since a date, with paging up to 500 per page, and it worked in live tests. There is no async export job; CSV exports exist only in the app.

checks.title: Webhook security and delivery reliability
checks.why: Webhooks carry a fixed per-account secret, obtained by contacting Latchel Engineering, not a signature. The published documentation shows no retry policy or replay guidance.

checks.title: Concurrency and conflict control
checks.why: The published documentation shows no ETag, version field, or conflict response. The docs warn that an update without the full contact list removes contacts, so the last write wins.

checks.title: Versioning and backward compatibility
checks.why: The version is in the path (/v1), but the published documentation shows no breaking-change definition, deprecation notice period, or deprecation signal. The terms allow changes without notice.

checks.title: Request traceability
checks.why: None of the 21 live responses carried a request or correlation id, and none is documented.

checks.title: Service availability and status transparency
checks.why: status.latchel.com redirects to Atlassian's marketing page. No SLA, uptime commitment, or availability page was found.

checks.title: Read-only credentials
checks.why: Latchel's docs say API keys have full access to your account, and the key panel has no read-only option.

checks.title: Scoped credentials
checks.why: There is one all-powerful company key, with no scope or permission controls.

checks.title: Multiple keys
checks.why: The key panel shows one key and a re-generate button, with no way to add a second key.

checks.title: Rotation and revocation
checks.why: You can re-generate the key yourself, and re-generating immediately invalidates the old one.

checks.title: Test environment and isolation
checks.why: A separate sandbox host with its own keys and data exists, and the development key used for this report's live tests worked only there. No first-party page explains how an operator gets a sandbox key, and webhook staging secrets require contacting Latchel Engineering.

checks.title: Delegated access
checks.why: The official hosted Latchel MCP uses standard OAuth: you sign in with your own Latchel account and approve what the connector can reach, with no API keys to manage. The Partner API itself has no OAuth.

checks.title: Complete self-serve reference
checks.why: A public reference backed by a complete OpenAPI file covers every endpoint with auth, parameters, request bodies, and field examples. Worked request and response examples are missing, most error responses are undocumented, and there are some schema defects.

checks.title: Reliable machine-consumable integration path
checks.why: A published, maintained OpenAPI 3.0 file covers the full Partner API, alongside an OpenAPI 3.1 webhooks file and an official read-write MCP server. There are no SDKs.

checks.title: AI-readable documentation
checks.why: The Help Center offers llms.txt, llms-full.txt, per-page Markdown, and a docs-search MCP server, but they cover only the API overview, key, and webhook pages, not the endpoint reference.

checks.title: Kept current
checks.why: Biweekly product release notes mention some API changes, and the spec is freshly dated. There is no API changelog, and several spec changes never appear in the release notes.

checks.title: Self-serve API key
checks.why: Latchel property managers can generate or regenerate an API key themselves in the Latchel console, under Account Settings, Integrations, and API Key.

checks.title: Not commercially gated
checks.why: API and MCP access are offered to Latchel property managers with no plan condition, and the verification search found nothing saying the API, webhooks, sandbox, or MCP are tier-gated or paid.

runs.agreement: 24 of 28 checks unanimous; 13 of 20 checklist items unanimous

disagreements.why: The API reads state and history and can cancel, approve, and deny, but has no general status update or completion endpoint. Run 2's 1.0 relied on actions documented only for the MCP connector.
disagreements.score_effect: part of the MCP question (see sensitivity)

disagreements.why: A vendor can be set only when a job is created, not on an existing job, and the MCP connector cannot assign a service provider either. The assignment exists but is materially limited.
disagreements.score_effect: none (Run 1 scored it 1.0 and still reached 87)

disagreements.why: The scheduled window is readable, but the API has no scheduling fields to update. Scheduling or rescheduling is documented only for the MCP connector.

disagreements.why: Estimate fields are read-only and filled in only while a job waits on approval. Approve or deny is scored in item 20, and adding an estimate is MCP-only.
disagreements.score_effect: 1.1 points of capability coverage, no grade effect

disagreements.why: Invoices can be listed and read, with an invoice webhook. They are vendor-submitted records, so reading them is what the item requires.
The API has owner records and budget approve or deny, but no owner-approval record. Recording an owner's approval or denial is MCP-only.

disagreements.what: Checklist item 17, transition its status to completion
disagreements.why: There is no completion endpoint, and a job update cannot set the status. Confirming completion is documented only for the MCP connector.
disagreements.score_effect: part of the MCP question (see sensitivity); this critical zero is one of the things that holds gate 2 at B

disagreements.why: The yes definition expressly includes a documented changed-since sync with paging. Latchel documents a Delta Sync with paging up to 500 per page, and it worked in live tests.
disagreements.score_effect: none (84 before the MCP step either way)

runs.summary: Runs 1 and 3 scored 87 (B+), and Run 2 scored 97 (A+). Run 2 counted actions documented only for Latchel's MCP connector (completing a job, scheduling, owner approval, and adding an estimate) toward checklist coverage; the resolution did not, because the methodology credits coverage for what is available through the API, and Latchel has a public API. C1.1 and C1.2 differed only because of the checklist items, and the C2.7 and C3.6 splits leave the score at 84 before the MCP step either way.

sensitivity: The methodology does not say outright whether an official MCP server's documented actions count toward checklist coverage when a public API also exists. If they did (Run 2's reading), coverage would be 86.36%, write coverage 83.3%, and no critical item would score 0, so the score would be 93 (A) before the MCP step and 97 (A+) after it. The report flags this for clarification in the next methodology version, so the answer applies to every vendor.

Keep properties, residents, owners, and vendors in sync through the API
Upload photos and files to a work order, including before and after shots

watch: The published documentation shows no API way to mark a work order complete
The published documentation shows no API way to schedule or reschedule a job
A vendor can be set only at creation; reassigning happens in the dashboard
The published documentation shows no way to read or post work-order notes
One full-access key per company, with no read-only or scoped keys
Re-generating the key breaks every integration that uses it
No duplicate protection on creates, so a retry can make two work orders
The "next page" link drops your page size and can skip records
No overwrite protection, no request ID for support, and no public status page
Webhooks use a fixed shared secret, not a signature, with no documented retries
bottom: Latchel is a maintenance-coordination and AI call-center service that sits alongside your PMS. It is not a PMS, a bank, or a trust-accounting system, and your PMS stays the system of record. Its Partner API is a clean, self-serve REST API with an OpenAPI file, a "what changed since" sync, and webhooks, so you can build intake flows that create work orders, keep your property, resident, and vendor lists in sync, and feed job updates into your own reports or automations. The biggest limit is that the published documentation shows no API way to mark a work order complete, schedule it, or change its vendor; those steps stay in the Latchel app, or partly in Latchel's Claude and ChatGPT connector, which needs a person to sign in. Plan for one all-access key per company, no duplicate protection on creates, and a "next page" link that drops your page size, and handle those in your build.
provider_fit: Latchel is an AI maintenance-coordination and AI call-center platform for residential property managers, sold as software plus a service on a per-door subscription, not a PMS or a bank. You still need your PMS, which stays the system of record, and Latchel integrates with PMSs such as AppFolio, Rentvine, Buildium, Rent Manager, Propertyware, and Yardi.
